title: Kyverno 的 CEL 准入成本究竟花在哪：Kubernetes 准入控制优化剖析
originalTitle: Optimizing Kubernetes admission control: Where Kyverno’s CEL admission cost actually goes
summary: Kyverno 团队对 Kubernetes 准入路径进行性能剖析，发现约 86% 的成本并不在 CEL 策略表达式求值环节，与其为求值而设计的预期相反。文章据此拆解 Kyverno CEL 准入开销的真实去向，为准入控制优化提供依据。
context: Kyverno 是 CNCF 生态主流的 Kubernetes 策略引擎，这项官方剖析对大规模集群的策略性能调优有直接参考价值。
contentHtml:
CNCF projects highlighted in this post

Kyverno’s CEL (Common Expression Language)-based engines exist to evaluate policy expressions. So when we profiled the admission path, we expected to find the bulk of the cost in CEL evaluation.

It was not there. About 86% of what the engine allocated went into preparing the object for evaluation, and almost none of it into evaluating policy.

We went looking because a public benchmark put Kyverno behind the alternatives. Those benchmarks measured the legacy ClusterPolicy JMESPath engine, which did have a real regression at the time, and the usual answer was to point people at the newer CEL-based engine instead. That answer was right but incomplete: we had not checked what the CEL engine itself was spending its time on.

This post is about where that performance cost came from, why it grew with the number of policies you deploy, and what removing it did. The fix ships in Kyverno 1.19.2.

Please read the limitations section before you quote any number here. And as always, run your own tests in your environments, for real-world accuracy.

What the profile showed

Kyverno’s CEL engines evaluate policies against a CEL activation: a set of variables your policy expressions can reference. One of those variables is request, the AdmissionRequest the API server sent, converted into the unstructured map form CEL understands.

Here is a heap profile of the ValidatingPolicy engine handling admission requests, before and after the change, by share of total allocated bytes:

Before, ConvertObjectToUnstructured accounted for 86.8% of everything the engine allocated. CEL evaluation itself barely registered. After, object conversion falls to 2.9%, and the largest single frame becomes evaluateWithData — the code that actually runs your policy expressions.

The same pattern shows up in the MutatingPolicy engine, which was paying a smaller but still substantial version of the same cost:

One caveat on reading those profiles: the post-fix benchmark completes more iterations in the same time because it is faster, so the two profiles have different absolute totals. Compare the shares, not the raw bytes. Per-request figures come from the benchmark table further down.

Why: the same object, converted once per policy

The API server sends the admitted object as raw JSON bytes. CEL cannot read bytes, so Kyverno parses them into the map form CEL understands before it can evaluate anything against them.

That conversion happened inside the loop over matched policies rather than before it. With the Pod Security Standards set, roughly 16 policies match a typical Pod creation — so Kyverno parsed the same Pod 16 times, same input, same output, every time. The cost grew with your policy count and with the size of the object being admitted: O(policies), where it should have been O(1).

The object does not change between policies. There was never a reason to convert it more than once.

The fix: convert once per request

The change moves the conversion out of the per-policy loop. Kyverno builds the CEL request value once, before the loop starts, and every matched policy reuses it.

Doing that without changing what policies see takes some care. The expensive part of the conversion is the admitted object itself, so Kyverno converts a copy of the request with that object temporarily blanked out — which leaves only cheap fields to walk — and splices the object back in afterwards. The same conversion code still produces the result, so the output matches what policies saw before rather than being a reimplementation that someone has to keep in sync by hand.

Keeping policy behavior identical

The first attempt used a single shared builder for every CEL engine. Testing caught that this quietly changed how policies behave, because the engines had never agreed on what request.object meant in the first place.

Validating and generating policies saw the object exactly as the API server sent it. Mutating policies saw a normalized version. The two also disagreed about what an empty object looks like to CEL, which matters for operations like DELETE where one side is absent.

Unifying them would have changed the result of expressions people already have deployed. That is a conversation worth having, but not one a performance fix should start on its own. So each engine keeps the contract it already had, sharing one fast implementation underneath.

Equivalence tests pin this down: they run the original code as the reference and compare its output against the new one field by field, across every request type, so any drift fails the build.

What changed

The benchmark calls the engine directly with a roughly 50 KB Pod and a varying number of matched policies. It times the engine alone — building the request value, matching, and evaluating CEL. It does not include the webhook round trip, the API server, or etcd, so these are not end-to-end admission latencies.

The MutatingPolicy engine improves on the same curve, from 258,943 to 52,689 allocations and 10.59 ms to 2.97 ms at 64 policies.

The slope is the point, not the headline multiple. Before the change, allocations grew about 63 times going from 1 policy to 64. After, about 10 times — and that residual growth is CEL evaluation, which is the work you deployed the policies to get. Object preparation is now constant per request instead of proportional to how many policies you run.

Practically: adding policies to a Kyverno deployment used to carry a hidden per-policy serialization cost on top of the evaluation you asked for. It no longer does.

Image verification too

The image verification engine had the same pattern, with its own private copy of the conversion code, so it got the same fix. The gain there is memory rather than speed: image verification spends most of its time fetching signatures and attestations over the network, and that part does not change.

How this compares to native admission policies

With the per-policy tax gone, it is worth asking where Kyverno’s CEL engine actually sits against the API server’s own ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

Running the same 16 Pod Security Standards policies through both engines on one cluster, the answer depends on how many policies you enforce:

At one policy, native is ahead: about 9.2 ms against Kyverno’s 12.8 ms. At the full 16-policy set, Kyverno is ahead: about 20 ms against native’s 29 ms.

Those numbers were measured on Kyverno 1.19.0, which predates the change described above. The Kyverno side of that chart should now be better than shown; we have not re-run the comparison.

The two engines pay their costs differently. Native dispatches each policy separately on the API server, so its cost grows with the number of policies you enforce. Kyverno pays once per request to receive the object over a webhook, and that cost is shared across however many policies then evaluate. With only a policy or two, native is ahead. Once you are running a realistic set, Kyverno matches it and can come out ahead.

That framing only became accurate with this fix. Kyverno’s cost was not fixed per request before it — it was per policy, which is exactly why the curve looked the way it did.

The CPU side is more one-sided. Under matched load, Kyverno’s engine used about 3.2 cores against the API server’s 8.2 for native. The surprise in the API server profile is that 67% of its CPU sits in the policy dispatch machinery while the actual CEL bytecode execution is about 5.5% — the cost is dispatching 16 policies and building an input for each, not evaluating them. And that load lands on the control plane, which you cannot scale horizontally the way you can scale a Kyverno deployment.

Both numbers come from a single-host setup where the webhook hop is loopback and effectively free. On a real multi-node cluster that hop costs real latency on every Kyverno request, which narrows the latency gap and matters most at low policy counts. The CPU finding does not depend on topology.

The legacy engine, briefly

The benchmarks that prompted this work measured ClusterPolicy, the older non-CEL engine, so it is worth saying what happened there.

We reproduced the regression across four releases, each on a fresh cluster, run in shuffled order over eight rounds so no version was systematically favored, and compared everything against 1.13.6.

The regression is real — between 12% and 23% depending on load — and it appears between 1.16.4 and 1.17.0. That is where the engine started copying its entire evaluation context on every checkpoint, in order to fix a separate bug where one rule’s data could leak into the next.

The fix keeps that guarantee but stops paying for it upfront: it takes a shallow snapshot and only copies a value when something actually writes to it. The benchmark returns to roughly its pre-regression level, and the rule isolation still holds, pinned by a test that fails on the old code.

This ships in 1.19.2 alongside the CEL work, and only there. The legacy engine is on its way out, so the effort belongs in the engine replacing it.

What this does not fix

  • The engine still pays one JSON round-trip of the admitted object per request, to preserve the raw, un-normalized parse that request.object has always exposed. Evaluating against the typed object, or a cheaper representation, would remove even that — but it would change what policies see, so it needs its own design.
  • Mutating policies thread full objects between policies rather than propagating a patch diff. A patch-only model is a substantially larger redesign and is not implemented.
  • Tail latency under sustained load on a single replica is not addressed by any of this, and we have not re-measured it since. If you have seen Kyverno’s p95 swing widely between runs at high load, that is a separate problem and it is still open.

Limitations

  • Single machine. Everything here reproduces the relationship between configurations, not the absolute numbers you would see on a 32-core server.
  • Most of this is a Go benchmark. The allocation and timing figures come from benchmarks driving the real engine loop, and the profiles come from those benchmark runs. They isolate the engine cleanly, and they exclude network, serialization at the webhook boundary, and etcd.
  • The engine comparison uses loopback, so the webhook network hop is excluded, and dry-run, so the etcd write is excluded.
  • The native side runs Kyverno’s generated policies, which is a faithful same-policy comparison rather than a hand-tuned native policy set.
  • Side controllers were disabled in these runs. Only the admission controller was active.

Reproduce it

The harness is in the Kyverno repository under docs/perf-testing/: the version ladder, the pinned Pod Security Standards policy set, the k6 scripts, and the cluster setup. The engine benchmarks live beside the code they measure, in pkg/cel/policies/vpol/engine and pkg/engine/context.

If you benchmark Kyverno and get a result you do not like, please publish it — with the method, the caveats, and the per-trial numbers.

Conclusion

Our mission at Kyverno is to be the best policy engine for Kubernetes and beyond. Admission control is a critical process in Kubernetes clusters, and a slow or misconfigured controller can impact cluster operations. Thanks to our community, we have fixed performance issues and added more tests. For future releases, we will be looking at improving concurrency and further optimization.

Thanks to Mustafa Erdinç, whose comparison of different Kubernetes policy engines motivated this work.

  • #17572 — build the request activation once per admission request
  • #17585 — hoist the request-map build in the image verification engine
  • #17565 — reduce engine context checkpoint copy cost

title: 如何在不受你控制的 Kubernetes 环境中支持你的应用
originalTitle: How to support your app on Kubernetes environments you don’t control
summary: CNCF 博客文章讲解如何为客户运行、不受你掌控的 Kubernetes 环境中的应用提供支持，并指出这与自己集群里运行应用是两回事。文章点出核心难点在于你无法控制集群配置、升级节奏和周边工具。
context: 面向需要为多客户集群交付和支持软件的团队，切中供应商难以掌控运行环境的常见痛点。
contentHtml:
CNCF projects highlighted in this post

Running an application in Kubernetes is one thing, but supporting that application in Kubernetes environments your customers run is something else entirely. You don’t control the cluster configuration, its upgrade schedule, the surrounding tooling, or the process for investigating an incident. But customers will still look to you when your application won’t install, an upgrade breaks, or a workload behaves differently in their environment than they expected.

That doesn’t mean customer-managed Kubernetes deployments can’t work, but it does mean support has to account for the variation you’ll see in real clusters.

No Two Customer Environments Are Alike

You’ll definitely have two customers (or more!) who both say they run Kubernetes and yet have very different environments.

One may run a managed Kubernetes service in a public cloud. Another may operate its own infrastructure. They may use different Kubernetes versions, networking configurations, ingress controllers, storage classes, image registries, security policies, observability tools, or access controls.

Those differences affect how your application deploys and how your team supports it. A chart that installs cleanly in your reference architecture may fail because a customer’s admission policies reject a required permission, their storage configuration doesn’t meet your application’s requirements, or their cluster runs a Kubernetes version you haven’t tested yet or no longer support.

Unfortunately, your customer still experiences that as a problem with your application. That’s why your team needs a documented view of what the application requires from the cluster, and what falls outside the support boundary.

At a minimum, customers need to know:

  • Which Kubernetes versions and distributions you support
  • Which permissions, policies, and cluster capabilities the application needs
  • What networking, ingress, DNS, certificate, secret management, and storage configuration the application expects
  • What resources the application needs to run reliably
  • Which logs, events, metrics, and configuration details your support team will need during an escalation. With bonus points for providing commands directly.

The goal isn’t to make every customer environment identical (you can’t). Instead, you need to define a supported operating model so every deployment doesn’t turn into a new discovery process for your customer support team.

Customers Won’t Upgrade on Your Schedule

Your application roadmap may assume customers will move to newer Kubernetes versions quickly. A quick reality check: most won’t.

Customers have their own release schedules, validation processes, maintenance windows, compliance requirements, internal dependencies, and risk thresholds. Even when they want to upgrade, their platform team may have a long list of cluster add-ons, integrations, and workloads to validate first.

Like any other software, Kubernetes and different components in its ecosystem change over time. APIs are deprecated and removed, version compatibility varies across control-plane and node components, and the upstream project supports release branches for only the three most recent minor releases.

Your team needs a compatibility policy that answers a few basic questions:

  • Which Kubernetes versions do you support today?
  • Which versions are approaching the end of support?
  • How much notice do customers get before you stop supporting a version?
  • What does a customer need to do if an application release depends on a newer Kubernetes capability?
  • Can you offer a documented workaround when a customer can’t upgrade immediately?

If the answer to every compatibility problem is to update Kubernetes, customers will quickly find that your support isn’t aligned with how they operate. Your team needs to explain what’s incompatible, why it matters, and the easiest path to return to a supported configuration.

Kubernetes Expertise Has to Be Customer-Facing

A general application support team can’t diagnose every Kubernetes issue. When a product runs inside a cluster your customer manages, customer-facing teams need enough Kubernetes depth to identify where the problem really lives.

That doesn’t mean every support employee has to operate production clusters. It does mean someone working directly with customers needs to understand the difference between an application issue, a deployment-configuration issue, and a cluster-level issue.

For example, a pod stuck in Pending may point to unavailable capacity, resource requests that don’t fit on available nodes, a scheduling constraint, or a policy that prevents placement. An image pull failure may involve registry access, credentials, network connectivity, or image policy enforcement. Those details determine who needs to take the next action and what evidence they need to act on it.

Your customer-facing team needs dedicated Kubernetes expertise that can:

  • Ask for the right diagnostic information early
  • Review Kubernetes events, pod status, and relevant logs
  • Identify when a customer platform, security, networking, or infrastructure team needs to get involved
  • Explain the issue in terms each stakeholder can act on
  • Escalate to engineering with enough environmental context to investigate effectively

Getting accurate answers to these questions matters because the person opening a support case may not own the cluster. The application team probably owns the deployment. A platform team probably owns Kubernetes. Security owns policies. Another infrastructure team may own networking, storage, or identity. Someone on your team needs to help move the issue between those groups.

Build for Variation

You can’t control every Kubernetes environment where customers run your application. You can control whether your support model treats that variation as expected or as a surprise.

So make sure you have a plan for it by:

  1. Defining what you support.
  2. Documenting the requirements that matter.
  3. Testing the Kubernetes versions and deployment conditions you commit to supporting.
  4. Setting a clear upgrade and deprecation policy.
  5. Making Kubernetes expertise available during onboarding, deployment, escalation, and ongoing support.

The support model changes when a provider manages the Kubernetes layer alongside the customer. Instead of troubleshooting an application across an unknown mix of cluster configurations, versions, networking, and add-ons, the provider and customer can work from a more clearly defined operating foundation.

title: 当同步窗口关闭时：Argo CD self-heal 如何跳过了迁移钩子
originalTitle: When a sync window closes: How Argo CD self-heal skipped the migration hook
summary: CNCF 博客复盘了一个真实案例：客户在同步窗口关闭期间推送版本，Argo CD 报告 sync 成功，但迁移钩子实际没有执行。文章逐步拆解了 self-heal 机制跳过该迁移钩子的具体过程与原因。
context: sync 窗口与 hook 的交互是 Argo CD GitOps 实践中的隐蔽坑点，对平台和运维团队很有参考价值。
contentHtml:
CNCF projects highlighted in this post

The uncomfortable question

A few days ago, a customer asked me a question that sounded simple: “Argo CD said the sync succeeded, so why didn’t our migration run?” They had pushed a release while a deny sync window was active. When the window opened, five regional Applications rolled out the same commit. Three of them ran the database migration. Two did not, and the new code spent the next 36 to 44 minutes talking to a schema it did not understand.

My first instinct was to blame something specific to their setup. I was wrong. It took me two days, a throwaway lab, and a careful read of the Argo CD source to see that this is not bad luck. It is a race, and with the right timing, anyone can lose it.

Synced, healthy, and wrong

What bothered me most was how normal everything looked. The two broken Applications were Synced and Healthy on the new commit. Their last operation said “successfully synced (all tasks run)”. If you only looked at the UI, you would have signed off on the release.

The setup itself was ordinary. One service, five regions, one Application per region, automated sync with prune and self-heal turned on. Production sat behind a deny window outside business hours, and the migration ran as a Sync hook Job, which is exactly how many of us were taught to do it.

The only clue was buried in the controller log. The two bad operations listed thirteen specific resources and carried a self-heal attempt count of one. In other words, Argo CD had not deployed a release. It had healed drift, and healing drift never runs hooks.

A lab you can break on purpose

I don’t trust an explanation until I can make the failure happen on demand, so I built the smallest setup I could.

The app was as plain as I could make it. One Application with automated sync, prune, and self-heal. A ConfigMap and a Deployment that carry a release string, so every release makes the app OutOfSync. And a migration that runs as a Sync hook, labelled with its release so I could see at a glance which one last ran:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migration
  labels:
    release: "v11"
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: Sync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo migrating schema to v11; sleep 3"]

The last piece was a deny window on the project, four minutes long and starting at the current minute, so I knew to the second when it would close.

My first attempt did not reproduce anything, and that turned out to be the most useful run of the day. The app’s periodic refresh landed in the same second as my trigger, won the race, and did a perfectly correct full sync. So I changed the script. I pushed release v11 while the window was active, and refreshed the app fifteen seconds before the close to push its next periodic refresh a couple of minutes out.

The app synced v11 in one second, and the UI looked spotless.

Then I opened the migration Job. It still said release: v10.

I reproduced it five times out of six. The failure was not rare. It only needed the wrong event to arrive first.

The first refresh wins

With debug logging on, the story was right there. Argo CD refreshes an Application for two very different reasons. A level-2 refresh comes from the reconciliation timer, roughly every two to three minutes, and compares the app against Git. A level-1 refresh comes from a change to a managed object and reuses what the controller already knows. When a window closes, nothing announces it. The next refresh of either kind simply finds that syncing is allowed again, and whichever kind arrives first decides what happens next.

During the window, the timer-driven refreshes keep comparing the new commit and record it in status.sync.revision, while the last real sync stays on the old commit. A level-1 refresh then uses that same recorded revision as the one to compare, checks it against itself in evaluateRevisionChanges, and concludes there are no changes. With no changes, alreadyAttemptedSync only compares the Application’s source, which has not changed either, so the controller decides it already synced this revision. With self-heal on, that means healing drift: a sync of only the out-of-sync resources, which is a partial sync, which skips hooks and writes no history.

A timer-driven refresh compares against targetRevision instead, notices that the last synced revision is older, and runs a normal full sync with hooks. The bug fits in one sentence. On the level-1 path, the last compared revision is mistaken for the last synced one.

A hook is not a guarantee

It is tempting to reach for a quick fix inside the hook model. Make the migration a PreSync hook instead of a Sync hook. Turn on the newer RunHooksOnPartialSync option. Shorten the window. From what I read in the code, none of these change the outcome. A partial sync skips every hook type, the new option is ignored for automated syncs, and self-heal is automated by definition. The race happens at every window close, whatever its length. I didn’t test these three, but the code leaves little room for doubt.

The real lesson is broader than this bug. A hook runs when a particular kind of operation runs. If the release can reach the cluster through any other kind of operation, the hook is a hope, not a guarantee.

Make the migration part of the desired state

The fix I now recommend is to stop treating the migration as a side effect of syncing and make it part of what gets synced. Remove the hook annotations, give the Job a sync wave that runs before the app, and give it a name that changes every release.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migration-v11            # change per release
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"

Now the migration is an ordinary managed resource. A new release brings a Job that does not exist yet, so any sync, partial or full, sees it as missing and applies it, and Argo CD waits for that wave to be healthy before it touches the next one. In my lab, the wave version went through the exact broken self-heal path, and the migration still finished, one second before the new ConfigMap and Deployment were applied. The previous release’s Job was pruned on the way.

There are a few details worth getting right. Use a unique name per release, such as the image tag in a Helm template, because a Job’s pod template is immutable. Keep prune on so old Jobs are cleaned up. Don’t set ttlSecondsAfterFinished, or Kubernetes will delete the Job, self-heal will see a missing resource, and your migration will run again. Keep migrations idempotent anyway. And try a deliberately failing migration in staging before you rely on this, because that is the one case I did not test.

Or let the timer decide

If changing every chart is not an option this week, there is a blunter tool. Turn off self-heal on the apps that run migrations.

syncPolicy:
  automated:
    prune: true
    selfHeal: false

I ran two apps through the same window to compare. Both made the same faulty “no changes” decision. The one with self-heal on deployed v11 without its migration. The one with self-heal off logged “Skipping auto-sync: most recent sync already to […]” and simply waited. About two minutes later, its timer-driven refresh compared against the real last sync and ran a full sync with the hook, and the v11 migration finished.

No manual sync, and no window of mismatched code and schema, because the app stayed entirely on the old release while it waited. The price is drift correction. Anyone who edits a resource by hand now leaves it OutOfSync until the next commit.

Trust the sync, not the timing

Sync windows, self-heal, and hooks are each reasonable on their own. Together they leave a gap that opens at every window close, and whether you fall into it depends on which event reaches the controller first. I don’t think you should have to win a race to get a correct release.

So I stopped letting a hook be the only thing that runs a migration. If the schema change is part of the desired state, every path that syncs the release also syncs the migration. We do not need to trust the timing. We need to trust what we put in Git.

References

  • Argo CD docs: Sync Windows
  • Argo CD docs: Resource Hooks
  • Argo CD docs: Sync Phases and Waves

title: OpenShell 加入 CNCF：以开放治理保障 Agentic AI 安全
originalTitle: Welcoming OpenShell to the CNCF: Open Governance to Secure Agentic AI
summary: 在 KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 上，CNCF 接纳 NVIDIA 捐赠的 OpenShell 为 Sandbox 项目。OpenShell 是一个用于保护和治理自主 AI 代理的开源运行时，项目将以开放治理模式推进 Agentic AI 的安全化。
context: 头部芯片厂商将智能体 AI 安全治理开源并捐赠给云原生基金会，显示 Agentic AI 安全正成为云原生社区的新议题。
contentHtml:
CNCF projects highlighted in this post

Today at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) welcomes OpenShell as a Sandbox project. NVIDIA has contributed OpenShell, an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous AI agents, to the foundation’s community-led home.

As organizations put AI agents to work, they need to give agents real capability without giving them unchecked access to data, secrets, or networks. This requires enforcement outside of the agents, right within the infrastructure that the agents run on. 

OpenShell does exactly that: it manages and monitors agent behavior, provides and enforces policy-based boundaries for what it can do. OpenShell is adopting Cedar, another CNCF project, as its policy language. It’s a great example of CNCF projects building on one another.

Why this belongs in the cloud native community

Agents are becoming part of cloud native infrastructure, and the layer that governs them should be shared, vendor-neutral, and open to everyone who depends on it. OpenShell already reflects that spirit. Core contributors from NVIDIA, Red Hat, Docker, and Canonical have worked on the project since its inception. Their early involvement, alongside many additional organizations adopting OpenShell shows broad industry agreement on the need for dependable controls for agentic systems.

“Open source is the foundation of enterprise trust. As agents become part of cloud native infrastructure, the controls around them need to be open, auditable, and built together with the ecosystem. Bringing OpenShell to the CNCF puts governance of the project in the hands of the community. Red Hat has always believed that innovation thrives where collaboration is open, and we’re excited to help steward OpenShell alongside NVIDIA and the broader ecosystem.”

— Chris Wright, Chief Technology Officer and Senior Vice President of Global Engineering, Red Hat

Contributing OpenShell to the CNCF as a neutral foundation is a natural next step to expand and grow the OpenShell project. It has adopted the CNCF Code of Conduct, runs a public RFC process, and follows a governance model with explicit vendor-neutrality commitments. By contributing OpenShell alongside partners and maintainers from across the industry, NVIDIA aims to make secure AI available to all, under the same open governance model that supports other CNCF projects.

Built for an ecosystem

No two organizations run agents the same way. They use different infrastructure, secret stores, inference providers, and governance practices, and those choices change over time. OpenShell is designed to fit this variety through well-defined extension points for providers, compute, governance and approval workflows, policy enforcement, isolation, and credential management. Teams can adopt it incrementally and swap in what they already run. It also gives vendors, integrators, and end users clear places to contribute.

What changes, and what doesn’t

OpenShell is moving from NVIDIA’s GitHub repository to a neutral organization, ai-openshell. Working groups and special interest groups will form around integrated components and cross-cutting topics such as observability.

The core engineering efforts from NVIDIA will continue, while we welcome contributions from other interested parties.

Ways to participate

Whether your organization already uses OpenShell or is just exploring it, contributing is the best way to shape its future. Areas where help is especially welcome include:

  • Extension implementations. Reference implementations for compute, credential management, inference, and logging, along with shared documentation and conformance tests so third-party integrations behave consistently.
  • Policy and governance patterns. Real-world approval flows, egress rules, and per-tenant policies, shared as examples or a policy library, plus feedback on the Cedar-based policy approach.
  • Isolation and platform coverage. Broader support across Linux, macOS, and Kubernetes, security reviews, adversarial testing, and vendor-neutral confidential computing work.
  • Observability. Consistent metrics, traces, and audit events aligned with OpenTelemetry.
  • Packaging and release engineering. Package maintenance, reproducible builds, SBOMs, signing, and CI, all of which support Incubation requirements.
  • Deployment at scale. Multi-tenancy, identity and access integration, and policy management workflows drawn from your own deployments.

Get involved

  • Join the community mailing list for notes and call invitations.
  • Find the project in the CNCF Slack channel #openshell-dev.
  • Watch the ai-openshell GitHub organization for new repositories, “good first issue” labels, and design proposals.

Contributors, end users, and people who are both are welcome. We look forward to building the future of open agent governance together.
